sn42.3:1.1: A “warrior” (_yodhājīva_) is a professional soldier. I have taken the liberty of using the name “Dustin” in honor of Dustin Cheah, my sponsor while making this translation in Qi Mei, Taiwan. Dustin (literally “Thor’s stone”) has the connotation of “valiant fighter”. | Together with the following discourses, these make up three of the four branches of the military: foot soldiers, elephant marshals, and cavalry. Sanskrit dictionaries acknowledge _grāmaṇī_ as a military officer as well as a village headman.
sn42.3:1.3: Kauṭilya (Arthaśāstra 10.3.28–31, Olivelle trans.) advises a king to urge his soldiers to battle by telling them “Your destiny shall be that of heroes”, rousing them with the verses, “Heroic warriors who lay down their lives in righteous wars will in a moment reach even beyond the worlds attained by Brāhmaṇas desirous of heaven through a multitude of sacriﬁces, through ascetic toil, and through numerous gifts to worthy recipients. A new cup ﬁlled with water, well consecrated, and covered with Darbha grass—may that not be his lot and may he go to hell who will not ﬁght for the sake of the sustenance provided by his master.”
sn42.3:2.7: Another instance of kamma at death influencing rebirth is found at [mn97:38.7](), where Dhanañjāni the corrupt tax collector has a deathbed conversion and goes to heaven. In Theravada circles today, it is commonly held that one’s mental state at death determines one’s rebirth. These examples show that this is true only in exceptional cases where one is actively making strong good or bad kamma at the time of death.
